lists.title: John and Abigail Adams on Educating John Quincy Adams (1758–1786)
lists.summary: From Philadelphia, Paris, Amsterdam and Braintree, John and Abigail Adams directed their son's education by letter. His father set the books: Thucydides in Greek, Sallust, Cicero, Tacitus and Livy for "Wisdom and Virtue", and Demosthenes and Homer rather than easy school authors. His mother set the moral frame: hardship forms "the Hero and the Statesman". John Quincy's own letters record what he actually covered at Haverhill (1785–86): Greek grammar by heart, the Greek Testament, Homer, Xenophon, Horace, Terence, logic and Locke, ending in an oral Harvard examination and a translation into Latin. This program takes from the Adamses the pairing of hard classical texts with explicit moral and civic purpose, parents who keep writing to direct study, and a real examination as the gate to college-level work.

lists.title: Boston Public Latin School: Course of Study (c. 1770–1860)
lists.summary: America's oldest school (1635) prepared Boston boys for Harvard with a ladder of Latin and Greek: Cheever's Accidence and Corderius, then Aesop, Eutropius and Nepos, Ovid and Caesar, and finally Virgil, Cicero's orations, Horace, the Greek Testament and Homer, with "making Latin", memorization and Saturday declamation throughout. The town's 1789 "System of Public Education" and Master Gould's own account of the 1820s course (both printed in Jenks's 1886 catalogue) show the same sequence surviving the Revolution. Its alumni included Franklin (briefly), Hancock, Samuel Adams, Robert Treat Paine and Emerson. This program adopts its graded Latin ladder, its daily memorization of poetry, and its public declamation as the core of the grammar-school years.

lists.title: University of Cambridge: From the Elizabethan Statutes to the Triposes (1570–1850)
lists.summary: Cambridge and Oxford were the models the colonial colleges copied, and Cambridge was the closer model. Harvard's founding generation were Cambridge men. John Harvard was an Emmanuel man, Emmanuel sent more graduates to New England than any other college, and Newtowne took the name Cambridge. The Elizabethan statutes of 1570 set a four-year B.A.: "the first year shall teach rhetoric, the second and third dialectic, the fourth shall add philosophy". Public professors read Quintilian and Cicero, Aristotle's logic, ethics and politics, Euclid and Ptolemy, Homer and Demosthenes, and Hebrew from the Scriptures. Harvard's weekly round of logic, rhetoric, ethics, mathematics, Greek, Hebrew and disputation was built on this plan. In practice the college tutor directed the reading, as Waterland's Advice to a Young Student (1730) shows: Burgersdicius and Euclid, then Locke and Rohault, then Pufendorf and Grotius, then Newton, with the classics and divinity running alongside. After Newton's Principia (1687) Cambridge became a mathematical university. From 1747–48 the Senate House examination printed an order of merit (wranglers and optimes), which became the Mathematical Tripos. Beside the mathematics every candidate faced "Locke, Paley, Clarke, Butler". Paley's Moral Philosophy (1785) and Evidences (1794) became the university's ethics and apologetics, and the Classical Tripos followed in 1824. This program takes from Cambridge the rhetoric → logic → philosophy order, a tutor-set monthly reading plan, and a hard mathematical core joined to moral philosophy.

Locke's Essay: each disputant offered a philosophical question often taken from Locke; freshmen had college lectures in 'Locke and logic' (1802)

College classical lectures (Calendar, 1802): an oration of Demosthenes, Lysias or Isocrates, a Greek play, Longinus, Cicero, Quintilian, and selections from Herodotus, Tacitus and Thucydides, with weekly Latin or English compositions
Analytical Society (1812; Babbage, Herschel, Peacock): translation of Lacroix's differential calculus (1816), and Leibniz's notation set in the Tripos by Peacock as moderator in 1817
Previous Examination ('Little-Go', established 1822): in the fifth term, the Greek Testament, Paley's Evidences of Christianity, and one Greek and one Latin author

Waterland's four-year table comes through Wordsworth's reprint, Appendix III. Wordsworth prints its months in four yearly blocks, and he notes that later editions put in substitutes such as Wallis's logic for Burgersdicius. I have not checked the 1730 printing against it. The account of the Schools, the 1772–92 questions, and the 1747–48 printed lists come from Ball, who draws on Wordsworth and Mullinger. The Previous Examination and Classical Tripos come from the Victoria County History. I have not checked them against the 1852 Cambridge Commission report on HathiTrust. The Emmanuel link is from Cambridge in America. John Harvard and Thomas Shepard were Emmanuel men, and Henry Dunster, Harvard's first president, came from Magdalene. Founding-era Americans at Cambridge include the Declaration signers Thomas Lynch Jr. (Caius) and Arthur Middleton. Pitt the Younger (Pembroke, 1773) is the model English statesman formed by this course.

lists.title: Eton and Arnold's Rugby: The English Public-School Classics
lists.summary: Eton trained English statesmen almost entirely through construing, repetition and verse composition, using its own Eton Latin Grammar and the house anthologies (Poetae Graeci, Scriptores Graeci, Scriptores Romani) together with Homer, Virgil and Horace. The Clarendon Commission (1864) recorded exactly what each division read. At Rugby from 1828 to 1842, Thomas Arnold kept the classics but made them serve moral and political understanding: Thucydides, Herodotus and Aristotle, modern history, divinity lessons and chapel sermons. He gave the Sixth Form real responsibility for the school, aiming to form "Christian gentlemen." This program adopts Eton's memorization and verse writing together with Arnold's ordering of goals: religious and moral principle first, gentlemanly conduct second, intellectual ability third.

lists.title: Benjamin Franklin, Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (1749) and Idea of the English School (1751)
lists.summary: Franklin's pamphlet for the Philadelphia Academy (the future University of Pennsylvania) proposes that youth learn "those Things that are likely to be most useful and most ornamental": a fair hand, drawing, arithmetic and accounts, geometry and astronomy, English taught through the best English prose stylists, and a history course out of which geography, chronology, morality, oratory, politics, logic, natural history, and commerce are drawn. Its footnotes are a small anthology of the education writers the Founders read (Milton, Locke, "Hutcheson" (really Fordyce), Obadiah Walker, Rollin, Turnbull), and the 1751 Idea of the English School sets out a six-class English course. This program keeps Franklin's English-language spine (grammar, reading aloud, rhetoric, letters, essays), his history-centered integration, and his practical arts, but keeps Latin and Greek for everyone as the classical tradition did, which Franklin himself made optional.

lists.title: Georgetown: John Carroll's Academy and the Jesuit Plan of Studies (1787–1820)
lists.summary: John Carroll, a St. Omer and Liège Jesuit and later the first Catholic bishop in the United States, issued his Proposals in 1787 and bought the Georgetown site in 1789. Classes opened in 1791–92 on the model of the Jesuit colleges he had studied and taught in. The Proposals promised to "unite the means of communicating Science" with guarding "the Morals of Youth": the three Rs, mathematics, and English grammar alongside the learned languages, "open to Students of Every religious Profession". The college later grew into the Ratio's ladder of rudiments, grammar classes, humanities or poetry, rhetoric, and philosophy, with French, Spanish, declamations, and public exhibitions. Georgetown is the program's main Catholic founding-era precedent: classical Latin and Greek with moral formation, the vernacular, and modern languages for a republic, a model already proven in the St. Omer education of Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the only Catholic signer of the Declaration.

lists.title: Harvard College: Admission and Course of Study (1642–1790)
lists.summary: Harvard's first printed rules, in New England's First Fruits (1643), admitted only a boy who could read Cicero "or such like classical Latine Author extempore", speak and write Latin in prose and verse, and decline Greek nouns and verbs. After that came a three-year weekly round of logic, physics, ethics and politics, arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldee and Syriac, rhetoric and declamation, catechetical divinity, history and botany, with disputations every week. The degree test was reading the Old and New Testaments in their original languages into Latin and "resolving them logically". By the 1767 laws Virgil and the Greek New Testament had joined Cicero at entrance, each tutor taught one subject, and Locke, Watts, 's Gravesande and Burlamaqui had come into the course. This program keeps that order. Cicero, Virgil and the Greek New Testament are the bar a student must clear before the college years. Hebrew is read in the Psalms and the Hebrew Bible. Weekly disputation and monthly declamation are standing exercises.

lists.title: Thomas Jefferson's Reading Lists (1771–1814)
lists.summary: Jefferson wrote reading lists all his life. There is the 1771 catalogue for a gentleman's private library (Skipwith), the graded course in Greek and Latin originals for his nephew Peter Carr (1785), the 1787 advice to Carr on conscience, Spanish and religion, the law student's day planned hour by hour (Bernard Moore, c. 1773, recopied for John Minor in 1814), and the daily timetable for his eleven-year-old daughter Patsy (1783). Taken together they show one pattern: ancient historians, poets and moralists read in the original, then English law and political theory, all built on daily discipline and exercise. This program adopts the order of the Carr course (history, then poetry, then moral philosophy) for the Latin and Greek tracks. It uses the Moore schedule as a model for the college-level day. The Patsy timetable serves as a precedent for a daily rotation of music, drawing, a modern language and letter-writing.

lists.title: John Stuart Mill's Education (Autobiography, 1873)
lists.summary: In the first two chapters of his Autobiography, Mill records how his father taught him at home in London. He began Greek at three and Latin at eight. Most of the Greek and Latin canon, Euclid and algebra, and a wide range of history came before twelve; Aristotle's logic, Hobbes and Ricardo's political economy came by thirteen or fourteen. His father also made him teach his younger sisters and brothers and give an account of his reading on their morning walks. Mill judged that this gave him "an advantage of a quarter of a century", but at twenty the training ended in a breakdown he blamed on analysis that had worn away his feelings, and Wordsworth's poems helped cure it. This program takes the pace and the spoken narration on walks. It also takes the warning, and forms the affections through poetry, music, worship and friendship alongside the intellect.

lists.title: King's College (Columbia): Johnson's Advertisement and the 1763 Plan of Education (1754–1785)
lists.summary: In 1754 President Samuel Johnson set out the lowest qualifications for entering King's College. A boy had to read and write well and know arithmetic through division and reduction. He also had to parse the first select orations of Cicero, the first books of Virgil's Aeneid, and the opening of St. John's Gospel in Greek. Johnson promised a course in "the Arts of reasoning exactly, of writing correctly, and speaking eloquently". It would also cover surveying and navigation, geography and history, husbandry, commerce and government, and natural history, leading "from the Study of Nature" to God. Under Myles Cooper, the Governors adopted a four-year Plan of Education in 1763. It is one of the richest classical reading lists of the colonial era: Sallust, Caesar, Ovid and Aesop; then Cicero's Offices, Terence and Xenophon; then Cicero's orations and De Oratore, Quintilian, Horace, Aristotle's Ethics and Poetics, Plato and the Iliad; and finally Livy, Tacitus, the Odyssey, the Greek tragedians, Thucydides, Herodotus, Longinus, Demosthenes, Isocrates, Hebrew, and Grotius or Pufendorf. John Jay (class of 1764) and Alexander Hamilton (c. 1773–76) studied under this regime. This program uses the 1763 plan as a model for the order of Latin and Greek reading in grades 9–12 and college.

lists.title: Abraham Lincoln's Frontier Self-Education (c. 1816–1850s)
lists.summary: Lincoln reckoned that "the aggregate of all his schooling did not amount to one year." What he learned he "picked up" from a small shelf of books read over and over: the Bible, Aesop, Pilgrim's Progress, Robinson Crusoe and Weems's Life of Washington. To these he added a speller and an arithmetic, then Kirkham's grammar at twenty-three, surveying manuals, the Indiana statutes and Blackstone, and finally Euclid, which he mastered as a congressman and circuit lawyer. His case shows that a few great books, deeply absorbed, can form a statesman's mind and prose. This program adopts his method of rereading, copying and reciting, of self-directed study, and of law and geometry as adult disciplines of reasoning.

lists.title: John Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693)
lists.summary: Locke's letters to Edward Clarke on raising a gentleman's son became the most-read English book on education in the eighteenth century and a direct source for the Founders' generation; Franklin cites it repeatedly in his 1749 Proposals. Locke ranks the aims as virtue, wisdom, breeding, and learning, in that order: a hardy body, habits formed early, reasoning with children, reading taught by play, modern language then Latin by conversation, a practical sequence of geography, arithmetic, geometry, chronology, and history, then ethics and natural law (Cicero's Offices, Pufendorf, Grotius), plus a manual trade, accounts, and travel. This program adopts his order of virtue before learning, his early-years regimen, his conversational method for modern languages, and his natural-law reading for civics, but not his low view of grammar drills, verse-making, and formal logic. Newman argues against that view in the Idea of a University (Discourse 7).

lists.title: James Madison's Books for Congress (1783) and His Course of Study (1769–1786)
lists.summary: On 23 January 1783 a committee chaired by James Madison (with Hugh Williamson and Thomas Mifflin) gave Congress a list of books "proper for the use of Congress". It runs from the law of nature and nations (Grotius, Pufendorf, Vattel, Burlamaqui, Wolff) through diplomacy, history of every nation, and politics (Plato, Aristotle, Hooker, Sidney, Locke, Montesquieu, Hume, Smith) to a large collection on America. Congress rejected it as too costly. Madison's letters show where this learning came from: Horace and prosody on entering Princeton, history and moral science with "a little divinity", then his requests to Jefferson in Paris for books on "ancient or modern federal republics". Those books fed his 1786 notes on ancient and modern confederacies, used in preparing for the 1787 Convention. This program uses the 1783 list as the model reading shelf for its civics-law and history tracks at the college level.

lists.title: McGuffey's Eclectic Readers (1836–1879)
lists.summary: The McGuffey Readers were the common reading course of nineteenth-century American schoolchildren. They moved from the Primer's phonics and moral tales up to the Fifth and Sixth Readers, which work as an anthology of English and American literature, oratory and Scripture, each piece set up with lessons in articulation, inflection and gesture. The selections below are taken from the 1879 revised edition, the one digitized on Project Gutenberg. They show what the series expected a young citizen to recite and admire: Shakespeare and Milton, Gray and Bryant, Webster and Patrick Henry, and the Bible. This program uses the Fourth to Sixth Readers as a graded source of memory work, elocution practice and short moral essays in the middle years, before the pupil reads the authors whole.

lists.title: John Henry Newman, The Idea of a University (1852/1873)
lists.summary: Newman's Dublin discourses, given for the founding of the Catholic University of Ireland, with his later lectures on "University Subjects", are the classic 19th-century English case for liberal education. Knowledge is its own end; a university forms a "philosophical habit" of mind; theology is a true branch of knowledge that no university may leave out; literature is the voice of human nature and cannot be purged of sin. Classical grammar, composition, and Latin writing are the elementary discipline behind all of it. This program adopts Newman as the theological and philosophical capstone of its liberal-arts design: exact grammar and Latin composition in the early years, Homer, Aristotle, Cicero, and Virgil as the "schoolmasters of all generations", the English classics (Protestant ones included), and a clear line between the gentleman that liberal knowledge produces and the saint that only grace makes.

lists.title: Noah Webster: Speller, Reader, Dictionary, and the Education of Youth (1783–1828)
lists.summary: Noah Webster set out to give the new republic its own schoolbooks. His Grammatical Institute had three parts: the speller (later the "Blue-backed" American Spelling Book), a grammar, and a reader, An American Selection. Beside these stand his 1788 essay "On the Education of Youth in America" and the 1828 American Dictionary. All of them joined literacy to morality and patriotism: fables and a moral catechism in the speller, Revolutionary orations in the reader, and Scripture-laden definitions in the dictionary. Webster argued that a child should "rehearse the history of his own country" from his first words. This program takes his idea that learning to read is learning to be a citizen. It does not follow him in shrinking the classics, and it keeps Latin and Greek for every pupil.

lists.title: University of Oxford: The Laudian Course and the Reformed Examinations (1636–1850)
lists.summary: Oxford and Cambridge were the models the colonial colleges copied, and Oxford's rule for most of this period was Archbishop Laud's code of 1636. A student spent four years before the B.A. His first year went to the public lectures in grammar and rhetoric. His second went to logic and moral philosophy. His third and fourth added geometry and Greek. From the end of his first year he disputed "in parviso" on questions of logic, grammar, rhetoric and morals, and he defended them "according to Aristotle, whose authority is to be supreme". The M.A. took three more years of geometry, metaphysics, history, Greek, Hebrew, astronomy and natural philosophy. By the 18th century the professors had mostly stopped lecturing. Aldrich's little logic and the college tutor carried the teaching, and the degree examination had become a farce. John Locke (Christ Church, 1652), Blackstone, Johnson, Bentham, Adam Smith and Gibbon all came up under this system, and C. C. Pinckney heard Blackstone's law lectures while at Christ Church. The Examination Statute of 1800 brought back real, public, ranked examinations. From 1807 the classical school, Literae Humaniores ("Greats"), became the course of English statesmen. By c. 1830–50 its set books were Aristotle's Ethics with his Rhetoric or Politics, some Plato, Butler, Herodotus, Thucydides, Livy, Tacitus and the Greek and Latin poets. This program takes from Oxford the pairing of logic with the Ethics, disputation as a standing exercise, and the Greats canon of history, philosophy and poetry as the capstone.

lists.notes: The 1636 course, the lectures and the disputations come from the Latin text of the Laudian Statutes (Griffiths, 1888). The English wording here is my translation. The account from 1800 to 1850, the Greats and pass-degree lists, and the Eldon and Knox anecdotes come from the 1852 Royal Commission Report (pp. 58–67). The Greats books are the Commission's description of what "the most distinguished Students" usually read. Oxford printed no official set-book list, and the list changed with the examiners. The 1850 school of Law and Modern History had not yet been examined when the report was written, so its text-books are the Commissioners' forecast. The 18th-century logic evidence is from Wordsworth. Wordsworth dates Aldrich to 1692, but the Internet Archive has a 1691 printing. Locke matriculated at Christ Church in 1652 and was a Student there until the Crown expelled him in 1684. Gibbon (Magdalen) and Adam Smith (Balliol) are the standard hostile witnesses to the idle professors. The Commission quotes Smith's line that most Oxford professors had "given up even the pretence of teaching".

lists.title: College of New Jersey (Princeton) under John Witherspoon (1764–1794)
lists.summary: In 1764 a freshman at the College of New Jersey had to compose grammatical Latin, translate Virgil, Cicero's Orations and the four Gospels in Greek, and know vulgar arithmetic. He then read Horace, Cicero, Lucian, Xenophon, Homer and Longinus, and future ministers began Hebrew. John Witherspoon, president from 1768, described the course in 1772. First came Latin, Greek, antiquities and rhetoric. Next came geography with the globes, the first principles of philosophy, and mathematics. The third year was chiefly mathematics and natural philosophy. In the senior year students read the higher classics and took moral philosophy. Every junior and senior heard the President's lectures on chronology and history and on composition and criticism. The lower classes gave orations each evening. Witherspoon's Lectures on Moral Philosophy close with a reading list that runs from Leibniz, Clarke, Hutcheson and Butler to Grotius, Pufendorf, Burlamaqui, Harrington, Locke, Sidney and Montesquieu. His Lectures on Eloquence hold up Demosthenes, Cicero, Livy, Sallust, Tacitus, Xenophon, Addison and Swift as models of style. James Madison took this course from 1769 to 1771 and stayed a further year to study under Witherspoon. This program adopts Witherspoon's capstone: moral philosophy that moves into natural law and politics, joined to daily practice in public speaking.

Witherspoon, Lectures on Moral Philosophy, and Eloquence (Philadelphia: Woodward, 3rd ed., 1810) (Internet Archive)
Maclean, History of the College of New Jersey, vol. 1 (1877): 1764 Account of the College, admission rules, 1772 Hebrew resolution (Internet Archive)

Secondary: Miller Center, James Madison: Life Before the Presidency

entries.text: Admission (1764 Account): compose grammatical Latin; translate Virgil, Cicero's Orations and the four Evangelists in Greek; know the principal rules of vulgar arithmetic
Freshman year (1764): Horace, Cicero's Orations, the Greek Testament, Lucian's Dialogues, Xenophon's Cyropaedia
Sophomore year (1764): Homer and Longinus; geography, rhetoric, logic and mathematics begun

Junior and senior years (1764): natural and moral philosophy, metaphysics and chronology; Hebrew for most, especially future ministers; seniors review the classics and part of the Hebrew Bible, with weekly syllogistic and forensic disputation
Witherspoon's course (1772): first year Latin and Greek 'with the Roman and Grecian antiquities, and Rhetoric'
Second year: a complete system of geography with the use of the globes, the first principles of philosophy, and elements of mathematics
Third year: chiefly mathematics and natural philosophy; astronomy taught on David Rittenhouse's orrery
Senior year: 'the higher classics', more mathematics and natural philosophy, and a course of moral philosophy
President's lectures to juniors and seniors: chronology and history, then composition and criticism (every student hears both twice)
Evening orations: the three younger classes speak from a stage in the hall after prayers; seniors give their own orations every five or six weeks

Prizes (commencement 1771): reading English with propriety and answering questions on its orthography and grammar; reading Latin and Greek with 'true quantity'; speaking Latin; Latin versions; English orations
French taught by the President to all who desire it (winter 1771–72); grammar school attached for Latin, Greek, writing and arithmetic
Hebrew (Trustees, Sept. 1772): 'of great importance' especially for divinity students; a tutor appointed to teach volunteers and the President to recommend it to all

Lectures on Moral Philosophy, reading list on the foundation of virtue: Leibniz's Theodicy, Clarke's Demonstration, Hutcheson's Inquiry and System, Wollaston's Religion of Nature, Butler's Analogy and Sermons, Reid's Inquiry, Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments, Beattie on Truth
Lectures on Moral Philosophy, writers on government and politics: Grotius, Pufendorf, Barbeyrac, Cumberland, Selden, Burlamaqui, Hobbes, Machiavelli, Harrington, Locke, Sidney

Recent political works: Montesquieu's Spirit of Laws, Ferguson's History of Civil Society, Kames's political essays, 'Grandeur and decay of the Roman empire' (Montesquieu's Considerations), Montagu's Rise and Fall of Ancient Republics, Goguet's Origin of Laws, Arts and Sciences

Lectures on Eloquence, ancient models: Demosthenes 'simple, close, nervous', Cicero 'flowing, fervent, ornate', Livy's narrative, Sallust's characters, Tacitus's observations, and Xenophon's 'dignity, elegance, and sweetness'
Lectures on Eloquence, English models: Addison for elegance and simplicity, Swift's political pieces for strength, Tillotson; critics Aristotle, Longinus, Quintilian and Rollin
Madison at Nassau Hall (1769–71, B.A. 1771): wrote home of commencement orations, disputes and dialogues; stayed a further year (1771–72) to study under Witherspoon

lists.notes: The 1764 course is from the Account of the College published under President Finley, as quoted by Maclean. It is the course Witherspoon inherited in 1768. The 1772 course is Witherspoon's own description in the Jamaica address. The Lectures on Moral Philosophy and Eloquence were student lecture notes, published after his death. Their 1810 preface says he never meant them for the press. The claim that Madison stayed on specifically to study Hebrew with Witherspoon comes from Madison's later autobiographical sketch as reported in secondary works. I could not verify it from a source I could fetch. Rives and the Miller Center confirm only the extra year of study, and the Founders Online documents could not be retrieved (automated access blocked). The 1772 Hebrew resolution shows the subject was voluntary but urged. French is tagged `spanish` only as the program's nearest modern-language track.

lists.title: The Jesuit Ratio Studiorum (1599)
lists.summary: The Ratio atque Institutio Studiorum Societatis Iesu set out the plan of studies for every Jesuit college: five lower classes (lowest, middle, and highest grammar, then humanities and rhetoric), a three-year Aristotelian philosophy course with Euclid, and a four-year theology course following St. Thomas. It was the curriculum behind St. Omer, where John Carroll and Charles Carroll of Carrollton were schooled, and behind Georgetown, so it is the main Catholic classical precedent in the founding era. This program takes over its sequence (grammar, then humanities, then rhetoric), its canon (Cicero above all, Caesar, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, the Greek orators and Fathers), and its methods: prelection, daily memory work, repetition, emulation, declamation, and academies.

primarySources.label: The Jesuit Ratio Studiorum of 1599, trans. Allan P. Farrell, S.J., 1970 (PDF, Educate Magis)
Farrell translation record (Loyola eCommons, Ignatian Pedagogy)
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911): Ratio Studiorum

entries.text: Lowest grammar: rudiments and beginning syntax from Alvarez's grammar; prelection on the easiest letters of Cicero; Greek reading and writing
Middle grammar: Alvarez Book II through figures of speech; Cicero's Ad Familiares and the simplest poems of Ovid; Greek catechism or the Tablet of Cebes
Highest grammar: full syntax and prosody; Cicero's letters, De Amicitia, De Senectute, Paradoxa; expurgated Ovid, Catullus, Tibullus, Propertius
Highest grammar poets: Virgil's Eclogues, Georgics IV, Aeneid V and VII; in Greek, Chrysostom, Aesop, and Agapetus
Humanities: Cicero's moral works, then simpler speeches (Pro Lege Manilia, Pro Archia, Pro Marcello); history from Caesar, Sallust, Livy, Curtius
Humanities poetry: Virgil (omitting some eclogues and Aeneid IV) and Horace's selected odes
Humanities Greek: Isocrates, Chrysostom, Basil, letters of Plato and Synesius, Plutarch; poems of Phocylides, Theognis, Gregory Nazianzen; compose in Greek
Soarez, De Arte Rhetorica (drawn from Aristotle, Cicero, Quintilian), summarized in humanities and taught in rhetoric
Rhetoric: daily prelection on Cicero's orations and Aristotle's Rhetoric (and, if desired, Poetics); 'Cicero is to be the one model of style'
Rhetoric Greek: Demosthenes, Plato, Thucydides, Homer, Hesiod, Pindar, with Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, and Chrysostom
Philosophy, year 1: logic (digest from Toledo or Fonseca; predicables, Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Topics)
Philosophy, year 2: Aristotle's eight books of Physics, On the Heavens, On Generation, Meteorology; mathematics from Euclid with geography and astronomy
Philosophy, year 3: Aristotle's On the Soul and Metaphysics; moral philosophy from the ten books of the Nicomachean Ethics
Scholastic theology over four years following the Summa of St. Thomas Aquinas
Sacred Scripture expounded 'reverently, learnedly, and seriously', with Hebrew taught for a year from rudiments through an easy book of Scripture
Cases of conscience (moral theology) for those training as confessors and pastors
Prelection method: read the passage, give its gist, clear each sentence, then comment; history read faster, poets by oratorical paraphrase
Daily memory recitation of grammar and Cicero to decurions (student monitors); repetition of the previous day's lesson
Concertatio: class contests between rivals and camps, with prizes, to rouse 'rivalry which is a powerful incentive to studies'
Declamations, plays, and student academies (rhetoric/humanities, grammar, philosophers/theologians) for speaking, disputation, and prelections

lists.notes: Titles, authors, and rules were checked against the Farrell (1970) translation. The rule on concertation is Rule 31 of the Common Rules for Teachers of the Lower Classes; the Scripture quotation is Rule 1 of the Professor of Sacred Scripture. The Ratio also prescribes expurgated editions of pagan poets. Fitzpatrick's St. Ignatius and the Ratio Studiorum (1933, trans. A. R. Ball) exists, but no online scan could be confirmed, so it is not linked. The Latin text (Pachtler, Monumenta Germaniae Paedagogica) was not located in this pass.

lists.title: Trinity College Dublin: The Undergraduate Course of Swift, Berkeley, Burke and Goldsmith (1637–1793)
lists.summary: Trinity College Dublin, with Oxford and Cambridge, was one of the models the colonial colleges copied. Its early provosts were all Cambridge graduates, and Laud's statutes (1637) gave it the same four classes an American college used: Junior and Senior Freshmen, Junior and Senior Sophisters. The science course ran logic (Porphyry, then Aristotle's Organon), physics, metaphysics and Aristotle's Ethics. Beside it ran daily Greek and Latin, a weekly Latin theme, declamations, syllogistic disputations in Hall, and an examination every term. Swift (1682–86) and Berkeley (from 1700) came through this course. Under Provost Ashe (1692–95) Locke's Essay became a Dublin text-book. The 1736 lists show what Burke (1744–48) and Goldsmith (1744–50) read: Burgersdicius's logic, then Le Clerc's logic and the Port-Royal Art of Thinking, then physics and geography, then Eustachius's Ethics, Pufendorf and metaphysics. In classics they went from Lucian and Sallust through the whole Iliad and Aeneid, Horace and Juvenal, Epictetus, Cicero's Offices and Livy, to Sophocles, Demosthenes On the Crown, Longinus and Tacitus. Burke's own debating club of 1747, the root of the College Historical Society, added what the course lacked: oratory, history and politics. The 1793 revision set Locke on Government and Burlamaqui's Natural Law in the final year, the same books as Revolutionary Harvard. This program takes from Dublin a term-by-term set-book list, examined every term, and a student-run society for declamation and debate.

primarySources.label: J. W. Stubbs, The History of the University of Dublin ... to the End of the Eighteenth Century (1889), incl. the Laudian course, the 1736, 1759 and 1793 lists, and the Historical Society (Internet Archive)
The Leadbeater Papers, vol. 2 (1862): Letters from Edmund Burke to Richard Shackleton from 1744, on his entrance examination and college reading (Internet Archive)
Letters of Edmund Burke: A Selection, ed. H. J. Laski (1922), incl. the 'furor logicus' letter of 1746–7 (Internet Archive)
Narcissus Marsh, Institutiones Logicae (Dublin, 1681), written for the Trinity undergraduates (Internet Archive)
Franco Burgersdicius, Institutionum Logicarum Libri Duo (1644 printing) (Internet Archive)
Francis Stoughton Sullivan, A Plan for the Study of the Feudal and English Laws in the University of Dublin (1761) (Internet Archive)
Murray's Compendium of Logic, the Dublin logic of the 1793 course, ed. J. Walker (1847) (Internet Archive)
Secondary: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Edmund Burke'

entries.text: Laudian statutes (1637), Freshmen: Junior Freshmen study logic, reading Porphyry's Isagoge through at least twice a year and examined daily; Senior Freshmen hear Aristotle's Organon explained 'as briefly as possible'
Laudian statutes, Sophisters: Junior Sophisters read Aristotle's Physics; Senior Sophisters his Metaphysics, and the Nicomachean Ethics in Lent term

Standing exercises (1637): a weekly written commentary on the lecture, a Latin theme or English-into-Latin translation every Saturday, declamations from memory in Hall on Fridays and Saturdays, and Greek lectures three mornings a week

Syllogistic disputations in Hall on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 2–4 p.m.: Freshmen on logic, Sophisters on natural philosophy and metaphysics; at the B.A., declamations in Greek and Latin 'in praise of philosophy' and syllogistic defence of questions in logic, natural and moral philosophy

Term examinations in Hall at the start of every term, judged in Logic, Natural Philosophy, Moral Philosophy, Greek, Latin and Theme; a roll of the 1680s shows Swift (identified by tradition) no better than 'mediocriter'
Narcissus Marsh, Institutiones Logicae (1681), the first text-book written for Trinity students, stating the inductive method 'more akin to Bacon than to the scholastic logic'

Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding: Provost Ashe (1692–95) 'ordered it to be read by Bachelors in the College, and strictly examined them' (Molyneux to Locke); later part of the undergraduate course

Entrance (Burke, April 1744): construe Horace's Odes, Aeneid VI from line 103, and Iliad III and VI before a Fellow; then examined 'very strictly' by the Senior Lecturer in the Odes, Satires and Epistles of Horace

Junior Freshmen, science (1736): Burgersdicius's Logic; Burke's first-term reading (1744) was 'nine first chapters of Burgersdicius, the six last Aeneids of Virgil, the Enchiridion of Epictetus, with the Tabula Cebetis'
Junior Freshmen, classics (1736): Lucian (Dugard's selection), Sallust, Iliad I–XII, the whole Aeneid, Hero and Leander with Theocritus, and Terence

Senior Freshmen (1736): Le Clerc's Logic, the Art of Thinking (Port-Royal Logic), selections from Smiglecius; in classics Iliad XIII–XXIV, Juvenal, Caesar's Commentaries, Epictetus with Cebes, Justin, Odyssey I–VIII and Horace

Junior Sophisters (1736): Colbert's General Physics, Le Clerc's Physics, Varenius's Geography and astronomy; in classics the rest of the Odyssey, Virgil's Georgics, Lucian, Cicero's De Officiis (Burke: 'I read for my College course Tully's Offices'), Velleius Paterculus, the Cyropaedia and Livy
Senior Sophisters (1736): Eustachius's Ethics, 'small Pufendorf' (On the Duty of Man and Citizen), Sanderson's Prelections on conscience and oaths, Baronius's Metaphysics

Senior Sophisters, classics (1736): Sophocles (Oedipus Tyrannus, Electra, Trachiniae), the rest of Livy, Aeschines and Demosthenes On the Crown, the Philippics, Suetonius, Longinus On the Sublime and the works of Tacitus
Scholarship examination (Burke, 1746): two days before the Provost and Senior Fellows 'in all the Roman and Greek authors of note'; Burke was examined in Catiline's speech in Sallust
Burke's study 'furors' (letter of 1746–7): natural philosophy, then 'logic and metaphysics' (the furor logicus), then history, then poetry, each 'very violent for a season, and very soon cooled'

Burke's Club (first meeting 21 April 1747): an oration every Tuesday; on Fridays a speech 'spoken off with proper emphasis and action' and a paper 'on a given topic in morality', to improve in 'speaking, reading, writing, and arguing in morality, history, criticism, politics'
College Historical Society (1770), heir of Burke's Club: each meeting opened with an examination in a set portion of history, followed by a debate with two appointed speakers on each side

1759 revision: twelve of Plutarch's Lives, Xenophon's Anabasis and Memorabilia, Euripides's Hippolytus and Iphigenia in Aulis, more of the Philippics and five orations of Cicero; Euclid entered the course only after 1758; entrance on fixed days in the whole Aeneid and fourteen books of the Iliad

Books the College prescribed for Dublin schools preparing boys for entrance (1759): Castalio, Erasmus's Colloquies, Nepos, Justin, Phaedrus, Caesar, Ovid, Sallust, Virgil, Cicero against Catiline, Terence, Horace, Juvenal; St Luke, the Cyropaedia, Iliad I–VIII, Hesiod, Theocritus; no literal translations, Latin verse, double translation, maps, English composition and 'the Common Rules of Arithmetic'
1793 course, Junior Freshmen: Murray's Logic, Aeneid VII–XII, Iliad XIII–XXIV, Horace's Odes, Euclid I–III, Virgil's Georgics, the Greek minor poets, Livy and Herodotus

1793 course, Senior Freshmen: Euclid V–VI, Locke's Essay (all four books), Livy, Plutarch's Solon and Lycurgus, Xenophon's Cyropaedia and Memorabilia, Caesar's Civil War, Plato's Crito, Apology and Alcibiades, Horace's Satires and Epistles

1793 course, Junior Sophisters: astronomy, mechanics, hydrostatics, pneumatics and optics; Juvenal, Persius and Lucian; Cicero's Orations, Demosthenes's Philippics and On the Crown, Aeschines Against Ctesiphon, and Quintilian

1793 course, Senior Sophisters: Burlamaqui's Natural Law, Conybeare's Defence of Revealed Religion, Locke on Government, Cicero's Offices; Tacitus, Thucydides, Terence, Sophocles, Plautus, Euripides and Longinus

lists.notes: Nearly everything here comes from Stubbs (1889), who prints the College's own lists of 1736, 1759 and 1793. Stubbs's text reads "Singlerius" (probably Smiglecius), "Clerk's Logic" (probably Jean Le Clerc), "Eustathius' Ethics" (probably Eustachius a Sancto Paulo), "Saunderson's Prelections" (probably Robert Sanderson) and "Wall's Astronomy". The identifications are mine, and I left the astronomy text unnamed. Burke's entrance, first reading list and Tully's Offices come from his own letters to Shackleton in the Leadbeater Papers. The furor letter is in Laski's selection. Burke entered on 14 April 1744 and took the B.A. in 1748. Goldsmith entered as a sizar in 1744 and took the B.A. in 1750. Swift entered in 1682 and took the B.A. in 1686. Berkeley entered in 1700. Berkeley's small private philosophical society anticipated Burke's Club. Berkeley later gave books to Yale and Harvard and endowed Yale's Berkeley scholarship, which is the direct Dublin–colonial link. The Club's minutes survive in Burke's hand, but I have not seen them. The quotations come through Stubbs, who took them from Walsh's 1864 address. Sullivan's 1761 plan is the programme of Dublin's first professor of feudal and English law, and I have not read it closely. I found no evidence that "Trinity College" meant Trinity College, Hartford (1823). The Burke, Swift, Berkeley and Goldsmith framing points to Dublin.

lists.title: George Washington's Education, Library, and Plan for a National University (c. 1745–1799)
lists.summary: Washington had no Latin, no Greek and no college. He was formed by a copybook of practical forms and the 110 Rules of Civility, and by practical reading: Seneca's Morals (signed at about seventeen), agriculture, military science and history. As president and in his will he pressed for a national university that would train young Americans at home in "the science of government". His letters to his step-grandson at Princeton (1796–97) are a founder's own advice on study habits and character. This program takes the Rules of Civility for early character formation, pairs practical arts (surveying, business forms, agriculture) with classical study, and follows Washington in treating civic education as a national duty.

primarySources.label: The Rules of Civility and Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation (Wikisource)
Moncure D. Conway, George Washington's Rules of Civility Traced to their Sources (1890), Project Gutenberg
A Catalogue of the Washington Collection in the Boston Athenaeum (1897), incl. inventory of Washington's library (Archive.org)

Farewell Address, 1796 (Avalon Project)

Last Will and Testament of George Washington, 9 Jul 1799 (Wikisource)

entries.text: School copybook 'Forms of Writing' (dated 1745): bills of exchange, bonds, receipts and sales copied out as penmanship exercises
Rules of Civility (copied c. 1745, aged about 14): 110 maxims copied by hand as a writing exercise and a code of conduct
Rule 1: 'Every Action done in Company, ought to be with Some Sign of Respect'
Rule 108: 'When you Speak of God or his Atributes, let it be Seriously & with Reverence'
Rule 110: 'keep alive in your Breast that Little Spark of Celestial fire Called Conscience'
Source of the Rules: a Jesuit courtesy book, Bienséance de la Conversation entre les Hommes (La Flèche to Pont-à-Mousson, 1595), probably through Francis Hawkins's English version (Conway)
Seneca's Morals by Way of Abstract (Roger L'Estrange, 1746 edition). Washington's copy is signed 'at the age of seventeen or thereabouts'
Addison's Cato. Washington attended a performance with his officers at Valley Forge in 1778
Mount Vernon library (executors' inventory at his death): Pope's Homer (Iliad and Odyssey), Pope's Works, The Spectator and Shakespeare
Mount Vernon library: Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding
Mount Vernon library: The Federalist, Smith's Wealth of Nations, and Gibbon's Decline and Fall
Mount Vernon library: Robertson's History of America and Charles V, and Sully's Memoirs
Mount Vernon library: husbandry. Washington made his own digests of Duhamel's and Tull's works on agriculture
Mount Vernon library: military treatises, including Simes's Military Course (listed as 'Simms's') and A Treatise of Military Discipline
Mount Vernon library: Bibles, including Bishop Wilson's Bible in three volumes, and sermons by Sharp, Jortin and Sterne ('Yorick')
First Annual Message (1790): 'Knowledge is in every country the surest basis of publick happiness'. He proposes aid to existing seminaries or a national university
Farewell Address (1796): 'Promote then, as an object of primary importance, institutions for the general diffusion of knowledge'. Religion and morality are 'indispensable supports'
Eighth Annual Message (1796): a national university would bring about 'the assimilation of the principles, opinions, and manners' of the country's youth. He also asks for a military academy
Will (1799): fifty Potomac Company shares toward a national university, so that youth need not be sent abroad and can outgrow 'local prejudices and habitual jealousies'
Will (1799): James River Company shares to Liberty Hall Academy, and a bequest to the Alexandria Academy to school orphans and poor children
Will (1799): enslaved children to be freed are to be 'taught to read and write' and brought up to a useful occupation
To G. W. P. Custis at Princeton (1796): 'The more knowledge you acquire', the greater your success and your thirst for more. Obey your tutors and respect the president
To Custis (1796): habits are forming now, and 'as the twig is bent so it will grow'. Guard 'the avenues which lead to idleness and vice'
To Custis (1796): 'True friendship is a plant of slow growth'. Be courteous to all but choose friends slowly, and allow recreation and 'manly exercise'
Custis to Washington (Nassau Hall, 1797): he reports reviewing Roman history, translating French, studying Hume and geography, and falling behind in arithmetic
To Custis (1797): keep to the course of study set by President Samuel Stanhope Smith, and aim to be accomplished in 'the useful and polite branches of literature'

lists.notes: Several items in the brief could not be verified because Mount Vernon's website (403) and Founders Online (bot challenge) blocked automated fetching, and the web search quota ran out partway through the research. Unverified and left out: Washington to Alexander Hamilton, 1 Sept 1796, on the university; the Farewell Address drafts; letters to Bushrod Washington; the Founders Online text of the Rules; and Mount Vernon's Washington Library pages. The library entries come from the executors' inventory of his books (made at his death) printed in the 1897 Boston Athenaeum catalogue, not from Mount Vernon. The claim that Washington "loved" Addison's Cato is supported here only by the Valley Forge performance, since his letters quoting Cato were not fetched. Conway's tracing of the Rules to a 1595 Jesuit source and the Hawkins translation is his 1890 argument. It is widely accepted but is secondary scholarship. Surveying and geometry exercises in the other school copybooks (c. 1745–47) are well attested but no primary text was confirmed online, so no entry is included for them.

lists.title: College of William & Mary: Charter, Statutes, and Jefferson's Reorganization (1693–1780s)
lists.summary: The 1693 charter founded William & Mary so that Virginia might have "a Seminary of Ministers of the Gospel". It was also meant to educate the colony's youth "in good Manners and Learning" and to carry the faith to the Indians. The statutes (first framed in 1727; printed in Latin and English in 1758) set up four schools. The grammar school taught Latin and Greek from the books used in English schools, plus the Church catechism. Two philosophy masters taught rhetoric, logic and ethics, and physics, metaphysics and mathematics. Two divinity professors taught Hebrew, exegesis, and commonplaces and controversy. An Indian school taught reading, writing and arithmetic. Jefferson studied there from 1760 to 1762. William Small gave the college's first regular lectures in ethics, rhetoric and belles lettres, and Small introduced him to George Wythe for the study of law. As a Visitor in 1779, Jefferson abolished the grammar school and the divinity and oriental-language chairs. In their place he set up professorships of law and police, of anatomy and medicine, and of modern languages. He added the law of nature and nations and the fine arts to moral philosophy. This program takes two things from William & Mary: grammar-school Latin and Greek finished before college, and the Founders' upper course in law, natural law, political economy, science and modern languages.

primarySources.label: The Charter, Transfer and Statutes of the College of William and Mary, in Latin and English (Williamsburg: William Hunter, 1758) (Internet Archive)
Jefferson, Autobiography (1821): studies under Small and Wythe; the 1779 reorganization (Avalon Project)
Jefferson, Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XV (Colleges): the professorships as they stood c. 1781 (Avalon Project)
Secondary: Herbert B. Adams, The College of William and Mary (U.S. Bureau of Education, 1887) (Internet Archive)

entries.text: Charter (1693): a college 'for Divinity, Philosophy, Languages, and other good Arts and Sciences', to supply a seminary of ministers; the Transfer (printed with it in 1758) restates the aim that youth be educated 'in good Manners and Learning'
Grammar school: Latin and Greek well taught, using the rudiments, grammars and classical authors 'used in the Schools of England'; the master must skip any passage against religion and good morals
Grammar school: all scholars learn the Church of England catechism in English, and the more advanced learn it in Latin
Examination in Latin and Greek before promotion from the grammar school to the philosophy school
Philosophy school: Aristotle's logic and physics no longer 'reigned alone'; the masters choose the systems of logic, physics, ethics and mathematics to teach
One philosophy master teaches rhetoric, logic and ethics; the other physics, metaphysics and mathematics; four years to the B.A., seven to the M.A.
Exercises: disputations, plus declamations and themes on various subjects (not taken from the Bible)

Divinity school: one professor teaches Hebrew and critically expounds the literal sense of Scripture in both Testaments; the other teaches the commonplaces of divinity and the controversies with heretics
Indian (Brafferton) school: reading, writing, vulgar arithmetic, and the catechism and principles of Christianity
Jefferson under William Small (1760–62): mathematics and natural philosophy, and the college's first regular lectures in ethics, rhetoric and belles lettres
Law under George Wythe: Jefferson read law under Wythe's direction after Small left in 1762. After 1779 Wythe held the new chair of law, and John Marshall attended his lectures
1779 professorship of Law and Police
1779 professorship of Anatomy and Medicine (Jefferson's autobiography adds chemistry)
1779 professorship of Natural Philosophy and Mathematics, with natural history added
1779 professorship of Moral Philosophy, the Law of Nature and Nations, and the Fine Arts (architecture explicitly included)
1779 professorship of Modern Languages
Jefferson's proposal: a future chair for 'the antient languages and literature of the North' (Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse), for their bearing on English language, law and history
Jefferson's Bill for Amending the Constitution of the College (1779, Revisal of the Laws): to enlarge the college's 'sphere of science, and to make it in fact an University'

lists.notes: The 1758 printing gives the statutes as amended by the Visitors between 1753 and 1756, with rules from 1742 added. Its preface says they keep the title and preface of the statutes first published, which are those of 1727. So the text here is the 1727 framework with mid-century amendments, not a clean 1727 text. I could not fetch or verify the text of Jefferson's Bill for Amending the Constitution of the College of William and Mary. Founders Online blocked automated access, so it is described only from Jefferson's Autobiography and there is no link. The six professorships come from Query XV of Notes on Virginia. The Brafferton kept its own place as the sixth. The modern-languages chair is tagged `spanish` only because the program's modern language tracks are Spanish and Chinese. The historical chair taught French, Italian and other modern languages. The `search` terms Blackstone, Vattel and Newton are cross-link hints, not texts named in the 1779 documents. Adams (1887) records Blackstone and Vattel as W&M texts only for 1830.

lists.title: Yale College: Admission and Course of Study (1726–1790)
lists.summary: President Clap's laws of 1745 set Yale's entrance bar: read, construe and parse Cicero, Virgil and the Greek New Testament extempore, write true Latin prose, know the rules of prosody, and know common arithmetic. Arithmetic was a new entrance requirement. Inside the college, the tongues and logic came first, then rhetoric, geometry and geography, then natural philosophy and astronomy, and last metaphysics and ethics. Saturdays were for divinity: the Westminster Confession, Wollebius and Ames. Students declaimed in Latin, Greek or Hebrew. When Ezra Stiles became president in 1778, he recorded the books each class recited: Virgil, Cicero, Horace, the Greek Testament, Ward's mathematics, Watts's Logic, Locke's Essay and Clap's Ethics. He also taught Hebrew to whole freshman classes himself. This program keeps Yale's order: languages and logic, then mathematics and natural philosophy, then moral philosophy. It makes Hebrew a Psalter-first discipline, as Stiles did.

primarySources.label: Yale Laws of 1745 (Clap), printed in Dexter, Biographical Sketches of the Graduates of Yale College, vol. 2 (1896), Annals 1745 (Internet Archive)
Orders and Appointments of the Collegiate School, as copied by Jonathan Ashley, 1726 (National Humanities Center excerpt of Dexter vol. 1)

entries.text: Admission (1745 laws): read, construe and parse Tully (Cicero), Virgil and the Greek Testament extempore; write true Latin prose; understand the rules of prosody
Admission (1745): common arithmetic, the first arithmetic entrance requirement at an American college
Admission (1726 orders): expert in Greek and Latin grammar, able to resolve Latin and Greek authors grammatically, and make good Latin
Daily private reading of Scripture, 'the Fountain of Light and Truth' (1745 laws); chapel with a chapter read morning and evening
Recitation exercise (1726): every class but freshmen reads Old Testament Hebrew into Greek in the morning and turns the New Testament into Greek at evening
Year 1 (1745): chiefly the tongues and logic; the tongues continued through the next two years
Year 2: rhetoric, geometry and geography. Year 3: natural philosophy, astronomy and other mathematics. Year 4: metaphysics and ethics
Saturday divinity: Westminster Confession, Wollebius's Compendium and Ames's Medulla Theologiae (1745); 1726 orders add the Shorter Catechism in Latin and Ames's Cases of Conscience on the Sabbath
Friday declamations in Latin, Greek or Hebrew 'and in no other Language' without leave; the two senior classes dispute twice a week (1745)
Speak Latin in chambers; no English among scholars except in public exercises (1726 orders)
Freshmen at Stiles's accession (1778): Virgil, Cicero's Orations, the Greek Testament, Ward's Arithmetic
Sophomores: Greek Testament, Horace, Lowth's English Grammar, Watts's Logic, Guthrie's Geography, Hammond's Algebra, Holmes's Rhetoric, Ward's Geometry, Vincent's Catechism on Saturdays
Juniors: Ward's and Atkinson/Wilson's Trigonometry, Greek Testament, Cicero's De Oratore, Martin's Philosophical Grammar and Philosophy (3 vols.)

Seniors: Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Wollaston's Religion of Nature Delineated, President Clap's Ethics; on Saturdays Wollebius, Ames's Medulla, Greek Testament (Edwards on the Will used at times)
Thomas Clap, An Essay on the Nature and Foundation of Moral Virtue and Obligation (1765), 'for the use of the Students of Yale College'

Hebrew under Stiles: he taught the whole freshman class from the alphabet through translating the first seven Psalms (June 1779), and later kept daily Hebrew recitations and moved on into the Hebrew Bible
Berkeley Scholar examinations (1780): candidates examined four hours in Horace, Cicero's De Oratore and Tusculan Disputations, the Greek Testament, the Septuagint and Homer's Iliad
Forensic disputation on live questions, e.g. seniors dispute 'Whether the present War be lawful on the side of America?' (Nov. 1779)

lists.notes: The 1745 laws are quoted from Stiles's manuscript copy as printed by Dexter. The 1726 orders come from the National Humanities Center's modernized excerpt of Dexter vol. 1. The claim that Stiles "made Hebrew required" comes from secondary sources, which also say he made it voluntary around 1790. His diary does show him teaching Hebrew to entire freshman classes, and I found no formal Corporation vote in the sources I checked. Stiles's 1779 book list describes the course "at my Accession", so it records the late Clap/Daggett course he inherited. The Hall (1894) summary of the 1720/1726 MS laws says "Wollaston's theology", which is probably a misreading of Wollebius, since the 1726 orders read "Wolebius".
